editorial.titleTr: Yongsan Park Being Reviewed Entirely for Apartment Development? A Century-Long Vision Must Be Considered
summaryTr: The government's review of converting the entire Yongsan Park into an apartment complex is drawing growing controversy.
As Seoul's last major urban park, its public value and historical significance must be carefully considered.
Before proceeding with housing supply, there is a need to build social consensus and pursue alternative solutions in parallel.
editorial.bodyTr:
The government is facing growing controversy as it reviews the entire Yongsan Park as a candidate site for housing development. As the last large-scale park in downtown Seoul with significant historical and environmental value, the development of Yongsan Park requires careful consideration of public interest, housing supply, urban competitiveness, and social consensus.

The government is currently keeping the entire Yongsan Park open as a housing supply candidate under review. Given that Yongsan Park holds great historical significance and value as a major park in downtown Seoul, the original intent of the special law and public interest are paramount. Since housing construction would be difficult to reverse once implemented, social discussion and consensus must come first, and alternative housing supply plans should be pursued simultaneously.

summaryTr: The Democratic Party launches a new leadership under newly elected Chairman Kim Min-seok.
The party must overcome internal conflicts from the primary process and shift focus toward people's livelihoods.
The ruling and opposition parties should work together to address real estate and state affairs issues.
editorial.bodyTr: A new party leadership has been formed with the election of Kim Min-seok as the new chairman of the Democratic Party. There are rising calls for overcoming the internal conflicts and policy distortions that emerged during the heated primary process, and for reestablishing the party's standing as a responsible ruling party centered on people's livelihoods. In particular, the party faces the challenge of moving away from legislative dominance and demonstrating a national governance partnership with cooperation between the ruling and opposition parties in addressing housing issues and other national affairs going forward.

editorials.titleTr: Editorial: U.S.-Korea Joint Military Drills Are Not Negotiable
summaryTr: President Trump has ordered a reduction in joint U.S.-South Korea military exercises.
Domestic political circles are seeking to use the drills as a negotiating card with North Korea.
The strength of alliances is fundamental to security.
editorials.bodyTr:
President Donald Trump's directive to scale back joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises has raised serious security concerns. The editorial emphasizes the fundamental significance and importance of these combined exercises, while critically analyzing how domestic political circles attempt to use them as a negotiating card in dealings with North Korea. It underscores that a solid alliance relationship is essential.

The joint military exercises between South Korea and the United States represent far more than routine drills. They serve as the backbone of our deterrence posture and a critical mechanism for maintaining readiness against potential threats. These exercises enable our forces to enhance interoperability, test operational procedures, and ensure that both allied nations can respond swiftly and effectively to any contingency on the Korean Peninsula.

The reduction of these exercises sends a troubling signal—not only to our military personnel who depend on this training, but also to potential adversaries who might interpret restraint as weakness. More concerning is the domestic tendency to view these exercises as mere bargaining chips in diplomatic negotiations. This reflects a dangerous misunderstanding of what these drills represent to regional security architecture.

The path to denuclearization and lasting peace on the peninsula must be built on a foundation of unwavering alliance strength, not on concessions that undermine our defensive capabilities. Weakening our readiness in hopes of improving dialogue is a false calculation that could invite miscalculation from adversaries.

The government must stand firm in affirming that robust joint exercises are non-negotiable elements of alliance management. Our security partnership with the United States cannot be compromised for short-term diplomatic gains.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Is the Government Ready to Break the Roh Moo-hyun Era Agreement to Turn Yongsan Park into Apartments?
summaryTr: The government is pushing ahead with plans to convert 20,000 units in Yongsan Park into apartments.
Amending special legislation will be necessary to break the 2007 Roh Moo-hyun administration's agreement to create green space.
It is problematic to ignore feasibility while chasing real estate supply targets.
editorial.bodyTr: The government is pushing ahead with a plan to build 20,000 apartment units in Seoul's Yongsan Park. As the real estate crisis deepens due to a cliff in apartment supply, the idea is to secure a large-scale residential site in central Seoul. While an initial proposal focused on a 300,000-square-meter children's garden within the 3-million-square-meter Yongsan Park, Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport Kim Yun-deok said on the 14th that the government would "review the entire Yongsan Park as a target for housing supply." While the government's urgency to "just push supply" is understandable, converting even the last large-scale green space in central Seoul into apartment complexes is a matter of a different dimension. Yongsan Park was established as a national park under the Yongsan Park Development Special Act enacted by the Roh Moo-hyun administration in 2007. It was a social promise to return the returned U.S. military base land to the public as green space. At that time, despite serious real estate concerns and some calls to build apartments, the consensus favored ensuring all citizens could benefit. The law includes a provision stating "the state shall not change the use or dispose of the main site for purposes other than a park." Breaking this social agreement and building housing would require an amendment to the special act. However, public opinion is negative, with thousands of objections to proposed amendments to change the park development plan. Many areas have not completed the U.S. military return procedures, and soil contamination cleanup remains an issue, so there are many obstacles to overcome before development can proceed. While the will to supply housing is necessary, it is problematic to chase supply targets without examining the feasibility of plans. The government has announced a plan to supply 1.58 million units through last year's September 7 measures and the recent August 13 measures, but there is almost no move-in volume during this administration's term. Prioritizing the acceleration of groundbreaking for existing projects and enhancing implementation capacity should come first. In Seoul, it makes sense to ease regulations on redevelopment and reconstruction projects and draw out private supply first. Minister Kim will meet with Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon, who has said "not even 1 centimeter of Yongsan Park should be damaged," on the 20th. Housing construction in Yongsan Park and the lifting of greenbelt restrictions are not matters the central government should push through by force or settle through confrontation. Only when real estate supply plans are created through sufficient consultation with local governments and social consensus can market trust be built.

editorial.title: AI-driven search shift
editorial.body: Google’s rise in Korea illustrates why portals like Naver must adapt to AI era For two decades, opening the internet in South Korea often meant opening Naver. In July, that habit slipped, exposing a deeper change in how Koreans find and consume information. Google’s mobile app recorded 47.02 million monthly active users (MAUs) in Korea, edging past Naver’s 46.85 million, according to Mobile Index. MAU measures whether an app was used at least once during a month, though it says little about time spent or search volume and excludes PC web traffic. Naver still holds more than 60 percent of traditional desktop and direct search traffic, compared with Google’s mid-30s share. The mobile figures therefore do not establish a new market order. They do, however, reveal where user behavior may be heading. Google has added about 8 million Korean mobile users in 18 months, while Naver’s growth has been much slower. Google has also pushed its Gemini AI deeper into search and mobile services. Features such as Circle to Search on Samsung Galaxy smartphones let users reach Google without opening a conventional search page. For years, Korean search revolved around major portals like Naver and Daum. Users entered through a portal site, typed keywords and worked through links, reviews and community posts. Generative AI is changing that routine. People can ask questions in ordinary language and receive synthesized answers, sometimes through images or voice. The search box is becoming an interface rather than a destination. ChatGPT’s growth adds weight to the shift. The AI chatbot developed by OpenAI recorded 16.46 million Korean MAUs in July, about 2.6 times Daum’s 6.31 million. A 2025 government survey found that 60 percent of generative AI users had shifted at least half of their conventional search activity to artificial intelligence. Against this backdrop, Naver faces a technological challenge alongside its market-share problem. Its strength was built on a dense domestic ecosystem of news, user-generated content, reviews and community knowledge. Yet a search environment crowded with sponsored results and promotional content can make useful information harder to find. Naver’s closed ecosystem also looks less compelling when AI systems can draw on the wider web. The consequences extend beyond Naver. Search traffic produces a steady stream of local, original information. If domestic platforms lose users, the supply of high-quality Korean data could shrink, weakening the foundation for locally developed AI. The AI-powered digital shift deserves attention from policymakers since data sovereignty is tied to the continued production and preservation of reliable domestic information, wherever users choose to search. Yet protecting Naver from competition would miss the point. Global tech firms spend tens of billions of dollars annually on computing infrastructure, chips and data centers. Expecting a Korean portal to match hyperscalers in general-purpose AI would be an expensive way to chase a losing game. Policymakers should instead focus on the conditions for competition. Korea needs cheaper access to computing power and energy, clearer rules for AI training and copyright. Regulations should also avoid weighing more heavily on companies simply because they fall within easy domestic jurisdiction. Naver also needs to reconsider where it can win. Its investment in Anthropic points toward cooperation with global AI developers, while its stronger advantage may lie in areas rich in Korean data and local networks. Korean portals should focus on logistics, commerce and other specialized services that offer more defensible opportunities than trying to replicate the largest AI foundation models. The July search numbers may reverse next month. What is harder to reverse is the change in how people look for information. Naver once owned the starting point of the Korean internet. 지난 20년간 한국에서 인터넷을 켜는 것은 대개 네이버를 여는 것을 의미했다. 7월, 이 습관에 균열이 생겼고, 한국인들이 정보를 찾고 소비하는 방식의 더 깊은 변화를 드러냈다. 모바일 인덱스에 따르면 구글의 모바일 앱이 한국에서 월간활성이용자(MAU) 4,702만 명을 기록해 네이버의 4,685만 명을 근소하게 앞질렀다. MAU는 한 달 동안 최소 한 번 이상 앱을 사용했는지를 측정하는 지표로, 사용 시간이나 검색량, PC 웹 트래픽은 포함하지 않는다. 네이버는 여전히 전통적인 데스크톱 및 직접 검색 트래픽의 60% 이상을 차지하고 있으며, 구글은 30대 중반의 점유율을 기록하고 있다. 따라서 모바일 수치가 새로운 시장 질서를 확립하지는 못했다. 그러나 이는 사용자 행동이 어디로 향할 수 있는지를 보여준다. 구글은 18개월간 약 800만 명의 한국 모바일 사용자를 추가했으며, 네이버의 성장은 훨씬 더디다. 구글은 또한 검색과 모바일 서비스에 제미니 AI를 더욱 깊숙이 밀어붙였다. 삼성 갤럭시 스마트폰의 서클 투 서치 같은 기능은 사용자들이 기존의 검색 페이지를 열지 않고도 구글에 접근할 수 있게 해준다.

수년간 한국의 검색은 네이버, 다음 같은 주요 포털을 중심으로 돌아갔다. 사용자들은 포털 사이트를 통해 들어가 키워드를 입력하고, 링크, 리뷰, 커뮤니티 게시물을 거쳐 정보를 찾았다. 생성형 AI가 이 루틴을 바꾸고 있다. 사람들은 자연스러운 언어로 질문을 던지고 종합된 답변을 받을 수 있으며, 때로는 이미지나 음성을 통해 받는다. 검색창은 목적지가 아닌 인터페이스가 되고 있다. 챗GPT의 성장이 이 변화를 뒷받침한다. OpenAI가 개발한 AI 챗봇은 7월 한국에서 1,646만 명의 월간활성이용자를 기록했으며, 이는 다음의 631만 명의 약 2.6배다. 2025년 정부 조사에 따르면 생성형 AI 사용자의 60%가 기존 검색 활동의 최소 절반을 인공지능으로 옮긴 것으로 나타났다.

이 같은 상황에서 네이버는 시장점유율 문제와 함께 기술적 과제에 직면해 있다. 네이버의 강점은 뉴스, 사용자 생성 콘텐츠, 리뷰, 커뮤니티 지식 등 밀집된 국내 생태계에 기반을 두고 있었다. 그러나 스폰서 결과와 홍보성 콘텐츠로 가득한 검색 환경은 유용한 정보를 찾기 어렵게 만들 수 있다. 네이버의 폐쇄적 생태계는 AI 시스템이 더 넓은 웹에서 정보를 끌어올 수 있을 때 덜 매력적으로 보인다.

그 결과는 네이버를 넘어간다. 검색 트래픽은 지역 정보와 원본 정보의 꾸준한 공급원이다. 국내 플랫폼이 사용자를 잃으면, 고품질 한국 데이터의 공급이 축소되어 국내에서 개발된 AI의 토대가 약해질 수 있다. AI 기반의 디지털 전환은 데이터 주권이 사용자들이 어디에서 검색하든 신뢰할 수 있는 국내 정보의 지속적인 생산과 보존과 연결되어 있기 때문에 정책 입안자들의 주목을 받을 만하다. 그러나 경쟁으로부터 네이버를 보호하려는 것은 핵심을 놓치는 것이다. 글로벌 기술 기업들은 매년 수백억 달러를 컴퓨팅 인프라, 칩, 데이터 센터에 쓴다. 한국 포털이 초대형 클라우드 서비스 제공자와 같은 수준의 범용 AI에 맞추길 기대하는 것은 지는 게임을 하는 비용이 많이 드는 방식일 것이다.

정책 입안자들은 대신 경쟁 조건에 집중해야 한다. 한국은 컴퓨팅 능력과 에너지에 대한 더 저렴한 접근, AI 학습과 저작권에 대한 더 명확한 규칙이 필요하다. 규제는 또한 단순히 기업이 국내 관할권 내에 있다는 이유로 더 큰 부담을 주는 것을 피해야 한다. 네이버도 어디서 승리할 수 있는지 재고할 필요가 있다. 앤쓰로픽에 대한 투자는 글로벌 AI 개발사와의 협력을 시사하는 한편, 더 큰 이점은 한국 데이터가 풍부하고 지역 네트워크가 강한 영역에 있을 수 있다. 한국 포털들은 물류, 전자상거래 및 기타 전문 서비스에 집중해야 하며, 이는 가장 큰 AI 기초 모델을 복제하려는 시도보다 더 방어 가능한 기회를 제공한다.

7월의 검색 수치는 다음 달에 바뀔 수 있다. 바뀌기 어려운 것은 사람들이 정보를 찾는 방식의 변화다. 네이버는 한때 한국 인터넷의 출발점을 소유했다. AI는 그 출발점을 소유하기를 훨씬 더 어렵게 만들면서 동시에 대안에 접근하기를 더 쉽게 만들고 있다.

editorials.title: AI-driven search shift
editorials.body: Google’s rise in Korea illustrates why portals like Naver must adapt to AI era For two decades, opening the internet in South Korea often meant opening Naver. In July, that habit slipped, exposing a deeper change in how Koreans find and consume information. Google’s mobile app recorded 47.02 million monthly active users (MAUs) in Korea, edging past Naver’s 46.85 million, according to Mobile Index. MAU measures whether an app was used at least once during a month, though it says little about time spent or search volume and excludes PC web traffic. Naver still holds more than 60 percent of traditional desktop and direct search traffic, compared with Google’s mid-30s share. The mobile figures therefore do not establish a new market order. They do, however, reveal where user behavior may be heading. Google has added about 8 million Korean mobile users in 18 months, while Naver’s growth has been much slower. Google has also pushed its Gemini AI deeper into search and mobile services. Features such as Circle to Search on Samsung Galaxy smartphones let users reach Google without opening a conventional search page. For years, Korean search revolved around major portals like Naver and Daum. Users entered through a portal site, typed keywords and worked through links, reviews and community posts. Generative AI is changing that routine. People can ask questions in ordinary language and receive synthesized answers, sometimes through images or voice. The search box is becoming an interface rather than a destination. ChatGPT’s growth adds weight to the shift. The AI chatbot developed by OpenAI recorded 16.46 million Korean MAUs in July, about 2.6 times Daum’s 6.31 million. A 2025 government survey found that 60 percent of generative AI users had shifted at least half of their conventional search activity to artificial intelligence. Against this backdrop, Naver faces a technological challenge alongside its market-share problem. Its strength was built on a dense domestic ecosystem of news, user-generated content, reviews and community knowledge. Yet a search environment crowded with sponsored results and promotional content can make useful information harder to find. Naver’s closed ecosystem also looks less compelling when AI systems can draw on the wider web. The consequences extend beyond Naver. Search traffic produces a steady stream of local, original information. If domestic platforms lose users, the supply of high-quality Korean data could shrink, weakening the foundation for locally developed AI. The AI-powered digital shift deserves attention from policymakers since data sovereignty is tied to the continued production and preservation of reliable domestic information, wherever users choose to search. Yet protecting Naver from competition would miss the point. Global tech firms spend tens of billions of dollars annually on computing infrastructure, chips and data centers. Expecting a Korean portal to match hyperscalers in general-purpose AI would be an expensive way to chase a losing game. Policymakers should instead focus on the conditions for competition. Korea needs cheaper access to computing power and energy, clearer rules for AI training and copyright. Regulations should also avoid weighing more heavily on companies simply because they fall within easy domestic jurisdiction. Naver also needs to reconsider where it can win. Its investment in Anthropic points toward cooperation with global AI developers, while its stronger advantage may lie in areas rich in Korean data and local networks. Korean portals should focus on logistics, commerce and other specialized services that offer more defensible opportunities than trying to replicate the largest AI foundation models. The July search numbers may reverse next month. What is harder to reverse is the change in how people look for information. Naver once owned the starting point of the Korean internet. AI is making the starting point much harder to own, while making alternatives easier to reach. Ex-PM Kim Min-seok takes DP helm DAEJEON ― Rep.
